fields.facts: Illinois benefit applicants sought future compliance and payment of benefits withheld during earlier violations.
fields.posture: Review of relief directed at state officials.
fields.issue: Could nominally equitable relief require retrospective payments from the treasury?
fields.holding: The retroactive monetary portion was barred by sovereign immunity.
fields.reasoning: The practical effect was liability payable from state funds for past conduct, unlike prospective compliance relief. Calling the remedy restitution did not change its effect. Participation in the federal program did not alone establish waiver.
fields.rule: Prospective compliance and retrospective monetary relief require separate immunity analyses.
fields.significance: Classify the actual financial and temporal effect of each remedy rather than relying on its label.

cases.title: Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 5 Essay Exam Notes, case brief section
cases.scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

fields.facts: State employees challenged discriminatory retirement benefits under Title VII as amended to cover state employers.
fields.posture: Question concerning congressional authorization of monetary relief against a state.
fields.issue: Could Section 5 enforcement legislation abrogate state immunity?
fields.holding: Yes, Congress could act under its Fourteenth Amendment enforcement authority.
fields.reasoning: The later Amendment directly limited state power and conferred enforcement authority. The source of congressional power therefore mattered to the immunity analysis.
fields.rule: Valid Fourteenth Amendment Section 5 legislation can support abrogation when the governing requirements are met.
fields.significance: Establish both the clear congressional intent and a valid constitutional basis; this case does not validate every statute labeled enforcement.

cases.title: Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 5 Essay Exam Notes, case brief section
cases.scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

fields.facts: State employees sought damages under the federal age-discrimination statute.
fields.posture: Review of whether the statute validly displaced state immunity.
fields.issue: Were clear abrogation language and the invoked enforcement power sufficient here?
fields.holding: The intended abrogation was not valid Section 5 enforcement as applied to the states.
fields.reasoning: The substantive constitutional protection against age classifications was narrower than the statute’s broad restrictions. The legislative record and remedy did not establish the required congruence and proportionality.
fields.rule: Clear intent and valid constitutional power are independent abrogation requirements.
fields.significance: Compare the constitutional right, evidence of state violations, and statutory remedy rather than stopping at express coverage of states.

cases.title: Gideon v. Wainwright
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 4, Gideon v. Wainwright
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: An indigent defendant requested counsel for a state felony trial. Florida denied appointment because the charge was not capital; he defended himself and was convicted.
fields.posture: Supreme Court review of the state conviction.
fields.issue: Did the state felony trial require appointed counsel for an indigent accused?
fields.holding: The Court recognized the fundamental right and overruled Betts v. Brady.
fields.reasoning: An adversarial criminal trial cannot reliably provide a fair contest where a person unable to afford counsel must face trained prosecution alone. The Sixth Amendment guarantee applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
fields.rule: Indigent defendants have the recognized right to appointed counsel for the state felony-trial setting at issue.
fields.significance: Distinguish this trial right from Miranda counsel safeguards and do not extrapolate appointment to every government encounter.

cases.title: Katz v. United States
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 6, Katz v. United States
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: FBI agents attached a listening device outside a public telephone booth and recorded Katz’s end of calls used in a wagering prosecution.
fields.posture: Review of a conviction upheld on the ground that agents had not physically entered the booth.
fields.issue: Could electronic interception constitute a search without physical entry?
fields.holding: The Court rejected the physical-entry limitation and found the surveillance constitutionally impermissible.
fields.reasoning: The conversation was something Katz sought to preserve as private despite the booth’s public accessibility. Visual exposure through glass did not mean his words were exposed for unrestricted listening.
fields.rule: Fourth Amendment protection is not confined to physical entry into a protected place.
fields.significance: Do not call every privacy interest a Fourth Amendment search; identify the actual governmental intrusion and the protected communication.

cases.title: United States v. Jones
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 6, United States v. Jones
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: Agents placed a GPS tracker on a vehicle and used it to monitor movements over several weeks.
fields.posture: Review following reversal of a drug conviction based on the tracking evidence.
fields.issue: Was installation and monitoring a search under the property-based theory?
fields.holding: Installation and use constituted a search.
fields.reasoning: Government physically occupied a protected effect to obtain information. Katz supplemented rather than eliminated the property-based protections of the Amendment.
fields.rule: An information-gathering physical intrusion on a protected person, house, paper, or effect can qualify as a search.
fields.significance: Keep property and privacy theories distinct. The search holding is not a universal resolution of every form of location surveillance.

cases.title: Terry v. Ohio
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 7, Terry v. Ohio
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: An experienced officer observed repeated walks past a store and conversations suggesting a planned robbery. He approached the men, frisked Terry, and recovered a gun.
fields.posture: Review of denial of suppression in a concealed-weapon prosecution.
fields.issue: Could the limited stop and weapons frisk be reasonable without a full arrest supported by probable cause?
fields.holding: The limited intervention was upheld on the particular facts.
fields.reasoning: Reasonableness depended on specific observations and the safety concern that the suspected robbers were armed. The scope of the frisk was tied to finding weapons rather than an unlimited search for criminal evidence.
fields.rule: A justified investigative stop and a justified protective frisk require their respective particularized grounds.
fields.significance: Explain the stop and frisk separately. Mere suspicion of crime does not automatically authorize a weapons search.

cases.title: Arizona v. Gant
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 7, Arizona v. Gant
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: After a suspended-license arrest, Gant was handcuffed and secured in a patrol car. Officers searched his vehicle and found cocaine in a jacket.
fields.posture: Review of the Arizona decision rejecting the asserted incident-to-arrest search.
fields.issue: Did the arrest automatically authorize the vehicle search?
fields.holding: The search was not justified by the asserted incident-to-arrest rationale.
fields.reasoning: Gant could not reach the car when searched, and the arrest offense did not supply a reasonable basis to expect relevant evidence in the car. The Court rejected an automatic search rule detached from those justifications.
fields.rule: A vehicle search incident to arrest requires the specified accessibility condition or the distinct reasonable-belief route for offense-of-arrest evidence.
fields.significance: Analyze both routes separately and do not silently substitute an inventory, consent, or general vehicle exception.

cases.title: Miranda v. Arizona
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 9, Miranda v. Arizona
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: Police questioned Miranda in custody and obtained a written confession without advising him of the right to counsel during questioning. A printed assertion of rights knowledge appeared on the statement.
fields.posture: Review of convictions affirmed by the Arizona court.
fields.issue: Were the interrogation statements admissible without the required safeguards and waiver?
fields.holding: The conviction was reversed; the statements were inadmissible under the stated framework.
fields.reasoning: Custodial interrogation threatened the privilege against compelled self-incrimination. Required warnings and a knowing, intelligent waiver could not be replaced by a boilerplate assertion in a signed confession.
fields.rule: The custodial-interrogation framework requires the recognized warnings or effective equivalent safeguards and an adequate waiver before use of resulting statements.
fields.significance: Analyze custody, interrogation, warnings, waiver, and invocation distinctly; do not infer waiver from a signature alone.

cases.title: Rhode Island v. Innis
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 9, Rhode Island v. Innis
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: After Innis requested counsel, officers transporting him discussed a missing shotgun and the risk to children. Innis interrupted and offered to show them the gun.
fields.posture: Review of the state court’s conclusion that the discussion was interrogation.
fields.issue: Was the conversation the functional equivalent of questioning under Miranda?
fields.holding: The Court found no interrogation on the circumstances presented.
fields.reasoning: The test includes conduct officers should know is reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, beyond routine custody conduct. The short discussion and what officers knew did not satisfy that test on this record.
fields.rule: Interrogation includes express questions and their functional equivalent under the reasonably-likely-to-elicit formulation.
fields.significance: Do not classify every police conversation within hearing as interrogation or limit the analysis solely to an officer’s asserted intent.

cases.title: Barker v. Wingo
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 20, Barker v. Wingo
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: Barker’s trial was repeatedly continued while the prosecution pursued a codefendant whose testimony it wanted. Barker did not object to many continuances.
fields.posture: Constitutional speedy-trial challenge after conviction.
fields.issue: How should lengthy delay be evaluated?
fields.holding: The Court adopted balancing and found no speedy-trial violation on this record.
fields.reasoning: Length, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice interact. The record indicated Barker did not truly want an earlier trial and did not establish the prejudice needed in the overall assessment.
fields.rule: The constitutional test balances the four identified factors rather than applying one fixed deadline.
fields.significance: Do not treat silence as automatic waiver or long delay as automatically conclusive; explain the weight of each factor.

cases.title: Faretta v. California
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., ch. 4, Faretta v. California
cases.scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: Faretta asked to represent himself before trial. The judge tested his legal knowledge and required representation by appointed counsel despite his stated choice.
fields.posture: Review of the resulting conviction.
fields.issue: Could a competent defendant make an informed choice to conduct the trial defense personally?
fields.holding: The Court recognized the right of self-representation in the trial setting.
fields.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment gives defense rights to the accused personally. Legal skill and an informed choice to surrender counsel are distinct; unwanted counsel cannot simply replace the defendant’s considered decision.
fields.rule: A legally sufficient knowing and intelligent choice can support trial self-representation despite lack of a lawyer’s technical ability.
fields.significance: Keep trial self-representation separate from appellate representation and later competency or procedural limitations not resolved by this brief.

cases.title: Martin v. Peyton
cases.locator: Macey, Moll & Hamilton, 14th ed., ch. 3, Martin v. Peyton
cases.scope: Decision reproduced in the supplied Macey, Moll & Hamilton casebook, 14th ed.; the syllabus assigns the 15th edition. Use the case citation, not an assumed edition-to-edition page match.

fields.facts: Creditors providing financial support to a brokerage firm received profit-related returns and contractual protections. Another creditor sought to treat them as partners.
fields.posture: Appeal from a judgment rejecting actual-partnership liability.
fields.issue: Did the financing arrangement make the lenders co-owners of a business for profit?
fields.holding: The court affirmed that the lenders were not actual partners under the agreement.
fields.reasoning: The arrangement had to be assessed as a whole. Profit participation could compensate a loan, and protective terms did not necessarily transfer the ownership role. A disclaimer of partnership was relevant but not conclusive.
fields.rule: The relationship’s substance controls; a share of profits is important evidence but not invariably determinative of partnership.
fields.significance: Identify meaningful co-ownership and management powers, not just profit-based compensation or a no-partnership label.

cases.title: Bartle v. Home Owners Co-op.
cases.locator: Macey, Moll & Hamilton, 14th ed., ch. 6, Bartle v. Home Owners Co-op.
cases.scope: Decision reproduced in the supplied Macey, Moll & Hamilton casebook, 14th ed.; the syllabus assigns the 15th edition. Use the case citation, not an assumed edition-to-edition page match.

fields.facts: A cooperative created a wholly owned construction subsidiary. After cost overruns and bankruptcy, the trustee sought to impose the subsidiary’s contract debts on the parent.
fields.posture: Appeal from refusal to pierce the subsidiary’s veil.
fields.issue: Did ownership and control justify charging the parent with these debts?
fields.holding: The refusal to pierce was affirmed.
fields.reasoning: Findings established maintained separate corporate indicia, no creditor deception, no fraud, and no injurious asset depletion. Forming an entity to obtain limited liability was itself legitimate.
fields.rule: Ownership and control alone do not necessarily supply the misuse or inequity required to disregard an entity.
fields.significance: Compare the claimant’s facts to actual abuse. Do not turn this result into immunity for every parent-subsidiary arrangement.

cases.title: Smith v. Van Gorkom
cases.locator: Macey, Moll & Hamilton, 14th ed., ch. 10, Smith v. Van Gorkom
cases.scope: Decision reproduced in the supplied Macey, Moll & Hamilton casebook, 14th ed.; the syllabus assigns the 15th edition. Use the case citation, not an assumed edition-to-edition page match.

fields.facts: Trans Union directors approved a cash-out merger. Shareholders challenged whether the board had adequately informed itself before approving the transaction.
fields.posture: Appeal from Chancery judgment for the directors.
fields.issue: Was the merger approval the product of an informed business judgment?
fields.holding: The judgment for directors was reversed; the Court found the decision uninformed.
fields.reasoning: The decision-making process, rather than merely the perceived attractiveness of the deal, was central. The record did not support the finding that the board had acted on an adequate informed basis.
fields.rule: Business judgment deference does not dispense with the governing duty to become adequately informed before deciding.
fields.significance: Compare the process challenge with Shlensky’s policy disagreement. Keep historical liability rules separate from any later exculpation analysis.

cases.title: Kirby v. Illinois
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 10, Kirby v. Illinois
cases.scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: The challenged identification was a showup conducted before indictment or other initiation of adversary judicial proceedings.
fields.posture: The supplied chapter discusses the Court’s refusal to extend the counsel rule to that pre-proceeding identification.
fields.issue: Had the Sixth Amendment assistance-of-counsel right attached at that point?
fields.holding: The Court refused to apply the identification counsel rule in that pre-proceeding setting.
fields.reasoning: Formal commencement marks the government’s commitment to prosecute and the point at which the Sixth Amendment prosecution-related guarantees attach. The Court distinguished the counsel inquiry from a due-process challenge to prejudicial identification procedures.
fields.rule: The Sixth Amendment counsel right attaches at or after initiation of adversary judicial criminal proceedings.
fields.significance: A failed Sixth Amendment argument does not eliminate a separate due-process challenge. Do not confuse Miranda safeguards with this attachment rule.

cases.title: Stack v. Boyle
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 13, Stack v. Boyle
cases.scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: Twelve Smith Act defendants received uniform $50,000 bail amounts. They offered individualized information, while the government relied on forfeitures by other defendants.
fields.posture: Review of unsuccessful efforts to reduce bail and obtain habeas relief.
fields.issue: Had bail been determined using methods appropriate to its permitted purpose?
fields.holding: The Court found the method improper and directed use of a renewed motion to reduce bail.
fields.reasoning: An amount above what is reasonably calculated to assure the particular defendant’s presence is excessive under the stated framework. The indictment and another person’s conduct did not replace an individualized assessment.
fields.rule: Bail must be set using standards relevant to assuring the individual defendant’s appearance.
fields.significance: Keep the historical federal bail framework and excessive-amount issue separate from an asserted unconditional constitutional right to release in every case.

cases.title: Arizona v. Hicks
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 7, Arizona v. Hicks
cases.scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: During lawful entry responding to a fired weapon, an officer moved stereo components to expose serial numbers and then discovered that equipment was stolen.
fields.posture: Review of whether the additional manipulation was a permissible plain-view inspection.
fields.issue: Could reasonable suspicion support moving the equipment to inspect concealed serial numbers?
fields.holding: The movement was a separate search and was unreasonable under the asserted justification.
fields.reasoning: Looking at already exposed details differs from physically manipulating objects to reveal concealed information. The Court rejected a new intermediate category allowing this additional search solely because it was brief.
fields.rule: Lawful presence does not itself authorize a new search to expose information not already in view.
fields.significance: Analyze initial entry, observation, manipulation, and seizure as distinct acts. Do not use plain view as a label for information exposed only by another intrusion.

cases.title: Georgia v. Randolph
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 7, Georgia v. Randolph
cases.scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: A physically present resident refused permission to search the shared home. Officers obtained consent from his wife, entered, and used the observations to obtain a warrant.
fields.posture: Review of exclusion based on the initial disputed-consent entry.
fields.issue: Did the other resident’s consent alone justify entry over the present resident’s express objection?
fields.holding: The Court upheld the rejection of the asserted consent justification on these facts.
fields.reasoning: Shared social expectations did not give one co-tenant’s invitation superiority over a present co-tenant’s objection. A separate safety justification would require its own analysis rather than reliance on the disputed invitation.
fields.rule: In the decision’s specified present-and-objecting setting, another co-occupant’s consent did not itself justify the entry.
fields.significance: Identify presence, objection, timing, scope, and the asserted exception. Do not state a rule for every absent-occupant or emergency situation from this brief alone.

cases.title: Apprendi v. New Jersey
cases.locator: Modern Criminal Procedure, 15th ed., chapter 27, Apprendi v. New Jersey
cases.scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

fields.facts: A firearm offense carried a ten-year maximum. After finding a bias-related purpose by a preponderance, a judge imposed a twelve-year sentence under an enhancement.
fields.posture: Constitutional challenge to the enhanced sentence after a guilty plea.
fields.issue: Could the judge’s finding authorize punishment above the maximum otherwise supported by the offense?
fields.holding: The Court rejected that allocation and standard of proof for the maximum-increasing fact.
fields.reasoning: Constitutional jury and proof protections concern the facts authorizing punishment, not merely whether the legislature calls them elements or sentencing factors. The decision stated a prior-conviction exception.
fields.rule: Other than the stated prior-conviction exception, a fact increasing the maximum must be submitted to a jury and proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
fields.significance: Find the maximum authorized before the disputed finding. Keep the assigned historical formulation separate from later sentencing developments not reviewed here.

cases.title: Elk Grove Unified School District v. Newdow
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 3 detailed notes, optional case discussion
cases.scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

fields.facts: Newdow challenged the school-led Pledge on behalf of himself and his daughter while the child’s mother disputed his litigation authority under the custody arrangement.
fields.posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.
fields.issue: Could he assert the child’s interests despite uncertain representative authority?
fields.holding: The Court declined to reach the constitutional merits on the standing-related ground described in the supplied notes.
fields.reasoning: The unsettled family-law relationship and competing parental authority made this an unsuitable vehicle for adjudicating the asserted rights.
fields.rule: A federal constitutional theory does not automatically resolve who may represent a child where domestic-relations authority is contested.
fields.significance: Distinguish the threshold ruling from a merits holding about the Pledge, and identify whose rights the claimant seeks to litigate.

cases.title: Murthy v. Missouri
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 3 detailed notes, optional case discussion
cases.scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

fields.facts: States and social-media users sought prospective restrictions on officials’ communications with platforms, alleging that government pressure caused moderation.
fields.posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.
fields.issue: Were the asserted future injuries sufficiently traceable to the named officials and redressable?
fields.holding: The Court found that the plaintiffs lacked standing on the record.
fields.reasoning: The claimed chain did not connect particular plaintiffs’ moderation injuries to particular official communications, and platforms retained independent incentives and choices.
fields.rule: An injunction claim involving independent intermediaries still requires concrete causal links and likely redress for the plaintiff.
fields.significance: Do not infer that the Court approved the challenged conduct; the threshold ruling left the constitutional merits unresolved.

cases.title: FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 3 detailed notes, optional case discussion
cases.scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

fields.facts: Doctors and associations who neither prescribed nor used the drug challenged FDA actions affecting others’ access to mifepristone.
fields.posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.
fields.issue: Did the challengers show the required personal injury, causation and redressability?
fields.holding: The Court unanimously found no standing and did not decide the FDA actions’ legality under the APA.
fields.reasoning: Moral opposition was not a personal injury; the asserted workload and conscience chains were insufficient on the record. An organization could not manufacture standing merely by spending money opposing a policy.
fields.rule: A policy disagreement or self-selected advocacy expense does not replace a legally sufficient injury connected to the challenged conduct.
fields.significance: Analyze standing before the merits and separate organizational injury from an attempt to sue on behalf of members.

cases.title: Alden v. Maine
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 5 detailed notes, optional case discussion
cases.scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

fields.facts: Probation officers pursued federal wage claims against Maine in state court after encountering immunity problems in federal court.
fields.posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.
fields.issue: Could Congress’s ordinary Article I commerce power authorize the private damages suit against the nonconsenting state?
fields.holding: The Court held that the asserted suit was barred by state sovereign immunity.
fields.reasoning: The immunity principle was structural and not confined to the literal party combinations or forum in the Eleventh Amendment’s text. Supremacy did not itself remove immunity.
fields.rule: Moving an ordinary Article I private damages claim to state court does not necessarily bypass a state’s immunity.
fields.significance: Keep this source-of-power problem separate from valid Fourteenth Amendment enforcement and specialized exceptions.

cases.title: Pennhurst State School and Hospital v. Halderman
cases.locator: Supplied Constitutional Law Module 5 detailed notes, optional case discussion
cases.scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

fields.facts: Residents obtained federal-court relief directing state officials to comply with duties based on state law.
fields.posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.
fields.issue: Could Ex parte Young support that order merely because relief was prospective?
fields.holding: The Court rejected the federal order enforcing state law against state officials.
fields.reasoning: The federal-law supremacy rationale for Ex parte Young did not support judicial orders based only on state law; supplemental jurisdiction did not override the immunity problem.
fields.rule: For the asserted official-capacity relief, prospective form alone does not suffice: the source of the violated duty matters.
fields.significance: Distinguish this 1984 state-law immunity case from the different 1981 Pennhurst decision listed as optional in the spending-power module.
